SECTION 1 – INTRODUCTION AND SAFETY

1.1 Scope. This manual covers the operation and maintenance of central plant assets under the
control of NMCS. It is intended for use by NMCS technicians and by contractors engaged under
the NMCS term maintenance contract. The manual is not a substitute for manufacturer
literature; where a conflict exists, the manufacturer’s instructions take precedence unless a
site-specific exception is recorded in Section 10 or in the asset log book.

1.2 Safety. Before commencing any work, carry out a dynamic risk assessment. Isolate
electrical supplies where required and follow the lock-off/tag-out procedure in NMCS HS-04.
Where work involves fire suppression systems, refer to Section 5 before opening any valve or
disconnecting any pipe.

1.3 Personal protective equipment. The minimum PPE for plant room work is safety
spectacles, safety footwear and hi-vis vest. Additional PPE is specified in the relevant section
of this manual.

1.4 Reporting defects. Any defect, leak, or abnormal reading must be reported to the Estates
Helpdesk on the same working day. If the defect affects a life safety system, also notify the
Fire Safety Manager by phone. Do not leave a defective system in service without a recorded
exception.

1.5 Training. Only personnel who have completed the NMCS in-house training module for the
relevant asset type may carry out maintenance. Refresher training is required every three
years. Records are held by the Training Officer.

SECTION 2 – FIRE SUPPRESSION SYSTEMS – GENERAL

The Fire Suppression System B7-2 suppression_agent is specified as Novec 1230 in the manual. Record status: current.

2.1 Types of system. The central plant includes the following fire suppression systems:

| System ref | Area protected | Agent | Type |
|------------|----------------|-------|------|
| B7-1 | Electrical substation 1 | Inert gas (IG-541) | Total flooding |
| B7-2 | Comms room and server suite | See Section 3 | Total flooding |
| B7-3 | Archive store | Inert gas (IG-01) | Total flooding |
| S1 | Open plan office (ground floor) | Water | Sprinkler |
| S2 | Workshop and stores | Water | Sprinkler |

2.2 General maintenance principles. All suppression systems must be maintained in
accordance with BS 5306 and the manufacturer’s instructions. Maintenance intervals are
given in the tables below. If a system is taken out of service for any reason, the Fire Safety
Manager must be informed in writing before the system is isolated.

2.3 Safety precautions. Never enter a protected space when the system is in manual mode
unless you are sure the discharge has been inhibited. Check the indicator panel before entry.
If the system has discharged, do not re-enter the space until it has been ventilated and the
atmosphere tested.

2.4 Spare parts. Keep a stock of commonly used spares, including seals, filters and pressure
gauges. Spare stock levels are listed in the Stores Catalogue. Any use of spares must be
logged on the stores issue sheet.

SECTION 3 – FIRE SUPPRESSION SYSTEM B7-2

3.1 General. The Fire Suppression System B7-2 protects the comms room and server suite in
the central plant building. The system is a total flooding gaseous system designed to
discharge within 10 seconds of detection.
Weekly: On the control panel, check the “SYSTEM NORMAL” indication is shown. Record
any fault or trouble indication in the log book. If the panel shows a fault, do not
silence the buzzer without first investigating the cause.

Monthly: Check that the cylinder pressure gauges read within the green band. Record
the actual reading. The pressure should be approximately 35 bar at 21 deg C. If the
pressure is low, contact the maintenance contractor; do not attempt to top up the
cylinder without authorisation. Also check the flexible discharge hose for kinks or
chafing.

3.6 Quarterly and six-monthly checks.

Quarterly: Using the test facility on the VESDA unit, introduce test smoke into the
sampling pipework. The panel should go into alarm within 60 seconds. Repeat for the
optical detectors using a smoke tester. Check the sounder/strobe units are audible and
visible. Check the manual release units are intact and the glass is not cracked.

Six-monthly: Carry out a functional test of the abort switch. With the system in
manual mode, operate the abort switch and confirm the panel shows “ABORT”. Release
the switch and confirm the indication clears. Check all pipework supports are secure
and that nozzles are not obstructed. Check the condition of all warning signs.

3.7 Annual check.

The annual check is to be carried out by the NMCS maintenance contractor or an
approved specialist. The following is a summary of the work:

1. Functional test of the full detection and release sequence using the test mode on
   the control panel. The discharge solenoid is not to be operated; the test is
   carried out by simulating the discharge signal.
2. Weigh each agent cylinder and record the weight on the cylinder test record sheet
   (Appendix C). Reject any cylinder that is more than 5% below the nominal fill
   weight.
3. Check the date of the last hydrostatic test on the cylinder neck. If the test is
   out of date, arrange for the cylinder to be replaced.
4. Visually inspect the discharge nozzles for damage or corrosion.
5. Check the condition of the flexible hoses and replace if the outer braid is
   damaged.
6. Check the control panel battery voltage and replace the batteries if below the
   manufacturer’s recommendation.

The installation record shows Fire Suppression System B7-2 installed_year as 2017. Record status: historical.
The annual check is therefore due in 2018 and every year thereafter.

cannot be cleared using this table, contact the maintenance contractor.

example, for building works), the following procedure applies:

1. Inform the Fire Safety Manager in writing, stating the reason and expected
   duration.

The agent used in Fire Suppression System DC-1 is argonite (IG-55). This is a blend of
50% argon and 50% nitrogen by volume, stored in the cylinder bank as a compressed gas
mixture. Argonite is electrically non-conductive and leaves no residue after discharge,
making it suitable for areas containing live electrical equipment and sensitive
electronics.

The Fire Suppression System DC-1 suppression_agent is listed as argonite (IG-55) in the

When replenishing agent cylinders, use only supplier-certified argonite (IG-55) meeting

bank for DC-1 comprises twelve 80-litre cylinders at a nominal fill pressure of 200 bar
at 15°C. The calculated design concentration for the protected volume is 38.2% by
volume. This concentration is maintained within the room for a minimum of 10 minutes
after discharge.

Cylinder pressure must be checked monthly. The acceptable pressure range is 190 bar to
210 bar at 15°C. If the pressure is outside this range, refer to Section 3.8 fault
finding. A pressure drop of more than 5% over a single month should be investigated
immediately for a possible leak.

**3.11 Discharge testing procedure**

Discharge testing is carried out to verify that the agent reaches the required
concentration and that the distribution is even throughout the protected volume. This
test is not the same as the annual functional test described in Section 3.7; a discharge
test actually releases agent from the cylinders.

Discharge testing is only permitted under the following conditions:

1. The area is evacuated and secured.
2. The Fire Safety Manager has issued a permit to work.
3. The ventilation dampers are closed and confirmed sealed.
4. The discharge is monitored using the pressure transducers at the test points shown
   in Appendix D.
5. The building management system is set to alarm mode so that a discharge signal is
   not misinterpreted as a real event.

The test procedure is as follows:

1. Isolate the system from the detection circuit using the key switch on the control
   panel.
2. Connect the test pressure transducers to the sample points. The sample points are
   located at ceiling level, at 1.0 m above floor level, and at the return air grille.
3. Record the ambient temperature and the room pressure before the test.
4. Operate the manual discharge control. The discharge solenoids will open and the
   agent will flow into the protected volume.
5. Record the pressure readings every 2 seconds for the first minute, then every
   10 seconds for the next 9 minutes.
6. After 10 minutes, record the final pressure readings and compare them with the
   predicted profile from the hydraulic calculation. The predicted profile is held in
   the system file, reference HYD-2016-044.
7. Ventilate the room thoroughly before allowing personnel to re-enter. The room must
   be ventilated for at least 30 minutes, or until the oxygen level is above 19.5% by
   volume.
**4.1 General**

All equipment rooms housing central plant assets shall be maintained within the environmental limits given in this Section. These limits are based on the manufacturer specifications for the installed equipment as well as on the requirements of the Building Management System (BMS) and the ventilation design. Where a more restrictive limit is given in a specific equipment manual, the more restrictive limit applies.

It is the responsibility of the Shift Supervisor to ensure that the environmental conditions in each equipment room are checked at the start of each shift and that any deviation from the limits in this Section is recorded in the Shift Log and reported to the Facilities Engineer on duty. The BMS provides continuous monitoring of temperature and humidity in the main plant rooms, but this does not replace the manual checks.

**4.2 Fire Suppression System DC-1 – Equipment Room Conditions**

The equipment room housing the Fire Suppression System DC-1 (the DC-1 room) contains the agent storage cylinders, the control panel, and the associated detection and actuation equipment. The room is located on the lower ground floor, adjacent to the main switch room.

The environmental limits for the DC-1 room are as follows:

| Parameter | Limit | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Minimum room temperature | 5 °C | Manufacturer specification. Current. |
| Maximum room temperature | 49 °C | Manufacturer specification. Current. |
| Relative humidity | 5% to 95% non-condensing | Manufacturer specification. Current. |
| Ventilation | Positive pressure, min 6 air changes per hour | See Section 4.5 |

The manufacturer specification requires Fire Suppression System DC-1 system_room_minimum_temperature to be 5 Celsius. Record status: current. This is the minimum temperature that shall be maintained in the DC-1 room at all times, including during periods when the heating system is being serviced or when the room is otherwise unoccupied.

If the room temperature is predicted to fall below the minimum limit, the Shift Supervisor shall arrange for temporary heating to be provided. Under no circumstances shall the system be taken out of service because of low temperature unless the temperature has actually fallen below the limit and the manufacturer has been consulted.

**4.3 Temperature Monitoring Procedure – DC-1 Room**

The temperature in the DC-1 room is monitored continuously by the BMS using the sensor located on the wall adjacent to the control panel. The BMS alarm is set at 6 °C and 48 °C.

In addition to the BMS monitoring, a calibrated portable thermometer shall be used to verify the room temperature at the following times:

1. At the start of each day shift, before any work is carried out in the room.
2. After any maintenance work that involves opening the room door for more than 30 minutes.
3. After any event that may have affected the room heating or ventilation, such as a power cut or a fault on the heating system.
4. At the end of each week, the weekly temperature check shall be recorded in the Weekly Plant Room Checks log (Form WPR-07).

The portable thermometer is held in the plant room office, in the drawer marked "Calibrated Instruments". The thermometer is calibrated annually; the calibration sticker is on the back of the instrument. If the thermometer is not available, the Shift Supervisor shall use the BMS reading and note on the log that the reading was taken from the BMS.
**4.4 Cooling Tower 2 – General Description and Duty**

Cooling Tower 2 (CT2) is a forced-draught, counter-flow unit serving the main process cooling loop. It is located on the roof of the plant room block, adjacent to the chiller yard. CT2 is the primary tower for the summer duty period; Cooling Tower 1 is retained as standby and for winter trim loads.

The tower is constructed from galvanised steel sections with a GRP basin. The fill pack is PVC, installed in 2017. The fan is a six-blade axial unit, belt driven from a 15 kW motor. The motor is controlled by a variable speed drive (VSD) located in the MCC panel on the plant room wall.

The datasheet gives Cooling Tower 2 cooling_capacity_kw as 1200 kilowatt. Record status: current. This rating is current and is the design figure used for all load calculations in this manual. The rating was confirmed at the last performance test (see Section 4.7) and shall be used for planning any future modifications to the cooling loop. The tower is not to be operated above this duty without written approval from the manufacturer.

Routine maintenance of CT2 is carried out by the NMCS mechanical team. The schedule below is based on the manufacturer's recommendations and on operating experience since commissioning. **4.6 CT2 – Detailed Maintenance Procedures**

**4.6.1 Fan Drive Belts**

Isolate the fan motor at the MCC panel before carrying out any work on the belts. Lock off the isolator and attach a warning notice. The belt tension is correct when the deflection at the centre of the top run is approximately 12 mm under moderate thumb pressure. Do not over-tension the belts, as this will shorten bearing life.

Inspect the belts for cracking, glazing, or fraying. Replace the belts as a matched set. When fitting new belts, do not use a lever to force them over the pulleys. The motor mounting bolts shall be loosened and the motor moved on its slide rails.
If fouling is light, the fill may be cleaned in place using a low-pressure water hose. Do not use high pressure, as this will damage the fill. If fouling is heavy, the fill pack shall be removed for cleaning or replacement. Refer to Section 4.8 for the fill pack replacement procedure.

**4.6.5 Basin Water Level and Strainer**

The basin water level is controlled by a float-operated make-up valve. The normal operating level is marked on the side of the basin with a painted line. Check the water level during the monthly inspection; it should be approximately 25 mm below the overflow weir.

The strainer is fitted at the suction side of the circulating pump. Clean the strainer by removing the lid and lifting out the basket. Rinse the basket and check for damage. Refit and ensure the lid seal is in good condition.

**4.6.6 Drift Eliminators**

The drift eliminators are located above the fill pack, below the fan deck. Annual inspection requires the fan to be isolated and the access hatch on the fan deck to be opened. Check the eliminator blades for cracking, warping, or displacement. Replace any damaged sections. Drift eliminator sections are Part No. DE-CT2-01.

**4.7 CT2 – Refrigerant System**

CT2 is fitted with a packaged air-cooled chiller for the closed-circuit cooling duty. The chiller is located on the plant deck, adjacent to the cooling tower basin. This section covers the refrigerant circuit, the refrigerant type, and the handling procedures.

**4.7.1 Refrigerant Type and Charge**

The chiller is charged with R-1234ze refrigerant. Cooling Tower 2 refrigerant_type is R-1234ze per the datasheet. Record status: current. This is the current and only approved refrigerant for this unit. Do not add or substitute any other refrigerant type without written authorisation from the NMCS Engineering Manager.

The refrigerant charge is 42 kg. The charge is recorded on the unit nameplate and in the chiller log book (Form CHL-02). A full charge record is kept in the plant office.

**4.7.2 Refrigerant Handling – General Precautions**

R-1234ze is a low-GWP (global warming potential) HFO refrigerant. It is classified as mildly flammable (A2L). The following precautions apply when handling this refrigerant:

- No smoking or naked flames in the vicinity of the chiller or any open refrigerant circuit.
- Work on the refrigerant circuit shall only be carried out by persons holding a valid F-Gas Handling Certificate (Category I or II as appropriate).
- The area around the chiller shall be well ventilated. If working indoors, ensure the area is mechanically ventilated.
- Use only refrigerant recovery equipment that is rated for HFO refrigerants. Do not mix recovery hoses or cylinders between different refrigerant types.
- Refrigerant cylinders shall be stored upright, secured, and in a cool, dry place. Do not store cylinders in direct sunlight.
- Spillages of liquid refrigerant can cause frostbite. Wear appropriate PPE, including insulated gloves and safety goggles.

**4.7.3 Leak Detection**

Leak testing of the refrigerant circuit shall be carried out in accordance with the F-Gas Regulation requirements. The chiller is fitted with a refrigerant leak detection system which alarms at a concentration of 10 ppm. The alarm is connected to the BMS.
**5.1 General**

This section covers the operation and maintenance of the main electrical distribution equipment in the central plant. It is intended for use by NMCS technicians and authorised contractors only. All work shall be carried out in accordance with the latest edition of BS 7671 (IET Wiring Regulations) and the Electricity at Work Regulations 1989.

Before any work begins on electrical equipment, the authorised person in charge of the work shall:

**6 PUMPS, VALVES AND PIPING SYSTEMS**

**6.1 General**

This section covers the routine operation and maintenance of the pumps, valves and piping systems installed within the Central Plant. It is to be read in conjunction with the relevant manufacturer's literature held in the plant office (drawing room, shelf B, binders P-01 to P-09). Where a conflict exists between this manual and the manufacturer's instructions, the manufacturer's instructions shall take precedence for equipment-specific details, but any deviation from the procedures herein shall be recorded on Form MP-04 and notified to the duty shift manager.

All work on plant items shall be carried out by competent persons. Isolation of any item for maintenance shall be in accordance with the Permit to Work system (Form PTW-01) and the site isolation procedure (Section 2 of this manual). Refer to the electrical isolation schedule for the relevant pump motor or valve actuator before commencing work.

**6.2 Pump Maintenance – General**

The following general procedures apply to all centrifugal pumps covered by this manual unless a specific exception is noted in the individual pump data sheets (Section 6.4).

**6.2.1 Routine Checks (Weekly)**

- Check pump for unusual noise, vibration or leakage from mechanical seal or gland.
- Check bearing housing temperature by hand. If too hot to hold (approx. 60°C or above), report and investigate.
- Check that the pressure gauge readings at suction and discharge are within the normal operating range noted on the pump data sheet.
- Check that the pump is not running dry. Confirm flow via the local flow indicator or duty point on the system.
- Visually check coupling alignment and condition of coupling guard.

**6.2.2 Lubrication**

Bearings are grease-packed and require no routine addition under normal service. The grease nipples shall be given one or two shots of grease (grade: Shell Alvania RL3 or equivalent) every 3 months for motors up to 30 kW, and every 6 months for larger machines. Do not over-grease; this can cause overheating and premature bearing failure.

The oil bath on the larger pumps (P-301, P-302, P-401, P-402) shall be checked weekly and topped up with the specified oil (see Table 6.4.1). A full oil change shall be carried out annually, or when oil analysis indicates contamination.

| **Oil Grade** | **Application** |
|---|---|
| Shell Tellus S2 V 32 | Bearing oil baths, all pumps |
| Shell Omala S2 G 220 | Gearboxes, if fitted |

**6.2.3 Mechanical Seals**

A small amount of seepage (a few drops per hour) from a mechanical seal is normal and indicates that the seal is being lubricated and cooled. A steady drip or spray indicates seal failure and the pump shall be taken out of service at the next available opportunity. Seal replacement shall be carried out only by a competent fitter familiar with the seal type fitted. Record the seal type and replacement date on the pump history sheet (Form MP-02).

**6.2.4 Pump Alignment**

Flexible coupling alignment shall be checked at the following intervals:

- After any major overhaul or disturbance of the pump or motor.
- When excessive vibration is reported.
- As part of the annual maintenance shutdown.

Use a dial gauge or laser alignment tool. The allowable misalignment is 0.1 mm total indicated reading (TIR) at the coupling periphery for speeds up to 1500 rpm, and 0.05 mm TIR for speeds above 1500 rpm. Shims shall be used under the motor feet to correct alignment; do not use more than 3 shims under any one foot. Record final alignment readings on Form MP-03.
**6.2.5 Vibration Monitoring**

Vibration readings shall be taken on all pumps and their drive motors using the handheld vibration meter (Brüel & Kjær 2239, located in the workshop cabinet, key held by the shift supervisor). Readings shall be taken at the bearing housings in the vertical, horizontal and axial planes. Record readings on Form MP-04.

|---|---|---|---|
| All pumps, 0–75 kW | Bearing housing, DE | 4.5 | 7.1 |
| All pumps, 0–75 kW | Bearing housing, NDE | 4.5 | 7.1 |
| All pumps >75 kW | Bearing housing, DE | 3.5 | 5.6 |
| All pumps >75 kW | Bearing housing, NDE | 3.5 | 5.6 |
| Drive motors, all sizes | Bearing housing | 4.5 | 7.1 |

If a reading exceeds the alarm level, repeat the measurement to confirm. If the reading is confirmed, increase the frequency of readings to weekly and inform the maintenance supervisor. If a reading exceeds the trip level, the pump shall be taken out of service and the cause investigated before further operation.

**6.2.6 Coupling Lubrication**

Flexible couplings (spider type, where fitted) require no lubrication. Gear-type couplings, where fitted (see individual pump data sheets), shall be lubricated with Shell Omala S2 G 220 grease every 6 months. Apply a sufficient quantity to fill the coupling cavity; do not overfill, as this can cause the coupling to overheat and throw grease.

**6.2.7 Safety Precautions – Rotating Equipment**

The following safety precautions apply to all work on pumps and associated rotating equipment:

- Isolate the pump electrically and mechanically (close and lock the suction and discharge valves) before commencing any work.
- Tag out the isolator with a personal danger tag and the pump control switch with a caution tag.
- Do not work on a pump while it is running. If work must be carried out on a running pump (e.g., taking vibration readings), ensure all guards are in place and do not wear loose clothing, ties, or jewellery that could become entangled.
- Ensure the coupling guard is in place before starting the pump. Do not operate the pump without the guard fitted.
- Use a suitable sling and lifting points when handling heavy components. Do not lift a pump by its coupling or piping.
- When draining oil, use a suitable container and dispose of the waste oil in the designated waste oil drum (located in the boiler house compound). Do not allow oil to enter the drains.
- When cleaning parts, use a degreasing agent suitable for the material. Do not use petrol or other flammable solvents.
- Be aware of hot surfaces. Pumps handling hot water (e.g., HWS circulating pumps) can have surface temperatures above 60°C. Use insulated gloves when working near these pumps.

**6.3 Air Handling Units (AHU-01 to AHU-06)**

**6.3.1 General**

The air handling units serve the office, laboratory and workshop areas. Each unit comprises a supply fan, a return air fan, a heating coil, a cooling coil (AHU-01, 02, 03, 05, 06 only), a filter section, and a fresh air intake. The units are located in the plant room on the roof of the main building, with the exception of AHU-04 which serves the workshop and is located at high level in the workshop itself.

**6.3.2 Routine Inspection**

The following inspections shall be carried out weekly:

- Check fan belts for condition and tension. A belt should deflect approximately 10 mm when pressed at the mid-point between pulleys. Replace worn or damaged belts.
- Check the drain pans for blockage. Clear any debris and ensure the drain traps are primed with water.
- Check the fresh air intake grilles for blockage by leaves or other debris.
- Check the condition of the flexible connections at the fan inlet and outlet for tears or leaks.
- Check the damper actuators for correct operation. The fresh air damper should open when the supply fan is running and close when it is not.

**6.4 Control System – General**

The central plant control system comprises the main control panel (MCP-01) located in the boiler house, two remote I/O panels (RIO-1 in the roof plant room, RIO-2 in the workshop), and the associated sensors and actuators. The system is a direct digital control (DDC) type, with a local operator display on the front of MCP-01. There is no remote access to the system; all adjustments are made locally.

Operators shall not make changes to control settings without authorisation from the Senior Technician. Any change shall be recorded in the Control Settings Log Book (kept on the shelf inside MCP-01).

**6.4.1 Operator Display**

The display shows the following values in sequence (or on demand via the navigation keys):

- Outside air temp
- Flow and return temps for each heating circuit (HWS1, HWS2, LTHW)
- Header pressure (HWS)
- Boiler status (on/off, fault)
- Pump status and running hours
- AHU supply and return air temps
- Filter differential pressure (AHU-01 to 06)

The display is a backlit LCD type. If the display is blank but the panel is powered, check the backlight fuse (F5, 500 mA) before calling for support.

**6.4.2 Time Clocks**

The control system has a 7-day time clock for each heating circuit. The clocks are set to give occupied and unoccupied periods. Check the clock setting each month against a reliable time source (e.g., the speaking clock or a GPS-synced watch). The clocks do not auto-adjust for BST/GMT – this is done manually by the technician during the spring and autumn changeover. If the clock is more than 5 minutes out, reset it and note the drift in the log book.

---

**6.5 Calibration of Sensors**

**6.5.1 General**

All temperature sensors and pressure transducers connected to the control system shall be checked for accuracy on a 12-monthly basis. The results shall be recorded on the Sensor Calibration Record sheet (Appendix C of this manual).

A sensor is considered acceptable if its reading is within the tolerances given in Table 6-1. If a sensor is outside tolerance, it shall be recalibrated (where possible) or replaced. Do not adjust a sensor without first checking the reading against a reference instrument.

**Table 6-1 – Sensor tolerances**

| Sensor type | Range | Tolerance | Reference instrument |
|-------------|-------|-----------|----------------------|
| Duct air temp (PT100) | 0–60 °C | ±0.5 °C | Calibrated digital thermometer |
| Pipe temp (PT100) | 0–120 °C | ±0.5 °C | Calibrated digital thermometer |
| Outside air temp (PT100) | −10 to +40 °C | ±0.5 °C | Calibrated digital thermometer |
| HWS header pressure (4–20 mA) | 0–10 bar | ±0.1 bar | Deadweight tester or calibrated gauge |
| Differential pressure across filters (4–20 mA) | 0–500 Pa | ±10 Pa | Manometer |
**6.5.2 Calibration Procedure**

Before starting any calibration work, isolate the sensor from the process where possible. For
duct and pipe sensors, remove the probe and allow it to stabilise at room temperature for at
least 10 minutes before comparing against the reference instrument. For pressure transducers,
close the isolating valve and vent the manifold to atmosphere to obtain a zero reading, then
apply a known pressure using the deadweight tester or a calibrated gauge.

Record the as-found reading on the Sensor Calibration Record sheet before making any
adjustment. If the sensor is within tolerance, record the reading and return the sensor to
service. If outside tolerance, attempt recalibration using the adjustment procedure in the
manufacturer's instruction leaflet (kept in the plant room filing cabinet, drawer 2). Where a
sensor cannot be recalibrated, order a replacement via the stores system and tag the faulty
unit with a red "OUT OF SERVICE" label. Do not leave a faulty sensor in service while waiting
for the replacement to arrive.

**6.5.3 Sensor Replacement**

When replacing a sensor, use only the type listed in the spares list (Appendix D). Check that
the replacement probe length matches the original before insertion. For duct sensors, ensure
the probe tip sits in the centre of the duct and is not touching the duct wall. For pipe
sensors, use the correct pocket and fill the pocket with heat-conducting compound before
inserting the probe.

After replacement, allow the sensor to stabilise for at least 15 minutes before checking the
reading against the reference instrument. Record the new sensor serial number and the date of
replacement on the Sensor Calibration Record sheet and in the log book.

---

**6.6 Control System Software and Firmware**

**6.6.1 General**

The control system runs on a proprietary platform supplied by the original control system
manufacturer. The software version currently installed is v4.2.1. This version has been in
service since March 2022 and has been stable. Do not upgrade or modify the software without
written authorisation from the Facilities Manager. Any proposed upgrade shall be reviewed
by the controls contractor and a risk assessment completed before work begins.

**6.6.2 Firmware Updates**

Firmware updates for the controllers (DDC panels) are issued occasionally by the manufacturer.
These updates are not automatically applied. The controls contractor shall assess each update
and advise whether it is applicable to this site. Updates that address a known fault or a
security vulnerability shall be prioritised. Other updates may be deferred until the next
planned shutdown.

Record all firmware updates in the log book, including the date, the version number before and
after the update, and the name of the engineer who carried out the work. A copy of the
manufacturer's release notes shall be filed with the log book entry.

**6.6.3 Backups**

A full backup of the control system configuration shall be taken every 6 months. The backup
shall be stored on a USB stick kept in the plant room safe and also uploaded to the shared
drive (folder: NMCS/Controls/Backups). The backup shall include the controller programs, the
graphics pages, and the trend logs.

After any significant change to the control system (e.g., a new time clock schedule, a change
to a set point, or a firmware update), a fresh backup shall be taken and the old backup
retained for at least 12 months. Do not overwrite the previous backup until the new one has
been verified as readable.

SECTION 1 – INTRODUCTION AND SAFETY

1.1 Scope. This manual covers the operation and maintenance of central plant assets under the
control of NMCS. It is intended for use by NMCS technicians and by contractors engaged under
the NMCS term maintenance contract. The manual is not a substitute for manufacturer
literature; where a conflict exists, the manufacturer’s instructions take precedence unless a
site-specific exception is recorded in Section 10 or in the asset log book.

1.2 Safety. Before commencing any work, carry out a dynamic risk assessment. Isolate
electrical supplies where required and follow the lock-off/tag-out procedure in NMCS HS-04.
Where work involves fire suppression systems, refer to Section 5 before opening any valve or
disconnecting any pipe.

1.3 Personal protective equipment. The minimum PPE for plant room work is safety
spectacles, safety footwear and hi-vis vest. Additional PPE is specified in the relevant section
of this manual.

1.4 Reporting defects. Any defect, leak, or abnormal reading must be reported to the Estates
Helpdesk on the same working day. If the defect affects a life safety system, also notify the
Fire Safety Manager by phone. Do not leave a defective system in service without a recorded
exception.

1.5 Training. Only personnel who have completed the NMCS in-house training module for the
relevant asset type may carry out maintenance. Refresher training is required every three
years. Records are held by the Training Officer.

SECTION 2 – FIRE SUPPRESSION SYSTEMS – GENERAL

The Fire Suppression System B7-2 suppression_agent is specified as Novec 1230 in the manual. Record status: current.

2.1 Types of system. The central plant includes the following fire suppression systems:

| System ref | Area protected | Agent | Type |
|------------|----------------|-------|------|
| B7-1 | Electrical substation 1 | Inert gas (IG-541) | Total flooding |
| B7-2 | Comms room and server suite | See Section 3 | Total flooding |
| B7-3 | Archive store | Inert gas (IG-01) | Total flooding |
| S1 | Open plan office (ground floor) | Water | Sprinkler |
| S2 | Workshop and stores | Water | Sprinkler |

2.2 General maintenance principles. All suppression systems must be maintained in
accordance with BS 5306 and the manufacturer’s instructions. Maintenance intervals are
given in the tables below. If a system is taken out of service for any reason, the Fire Safety
Manager must be informed in writing before the system is isolated.

2.3 Safety precautions. Never enter a protected space when the system is in manual mode
unless you are sure the discharge has been inhibited. Check the indicator panel before entry.
If the system has discharged, do not re-enter the space until it has been ventilated and the
atmosphere tested.

2.4 Spare parts. Keep a stock of commonly used spares, including seals, filters and pressure
gauges. Spare stock levels are listed in the Stores Catalogue. Any use of spares must be
logged on the stores issue sheet.

SECTION 3 – FIRE SUPPRESSION SYSTEM B7-2

3.1 General. The Fire Suppression System B7-2 protects the comms room and server suite in
the central plant building. The system is a total flooding gaseous system designed to
discharge within 10 seconds of detection.

Weekly: On the control panel, check the “SYSTEM NORMAL” indication is shown. Record
any fault or trouble indication in the log book. If the panel shows a fault, do not
silence the buzzer without first investigating the cause.

Monthly: Check that the cylinder pressure gauges read within the green band. Record
the actual reading. The pressure should be approximately 35 bar at 21 deg C. If the
pressure is low, contact the maintenance contractor; do not attempt to top up the
cylinder without authorisation. Also check the flexible discharge hose for kinks or
chafing.

3.6 Quarterly and six-monthly checks.

Quarterly: Using the test facility on the VESDA unit, introduce test smoke into the
sampling pipework. The panel should go into alarm within 60 seconds. Repeat for the
optical detectors using a smoke tester. Check the sounder/strobe units are audible and
visible. Check the manual release units are intact and the glass is not cracked.

Six-monthly: Carry out a functional test of the abort switch. With the system in
manual mode, operate the abort switch and confirm the panel shows “ABORT”. Release
the switch and confirm the indication clears. Check all pipework supports are secure
and that nozzles are not obstructed. Check the condition of all warning signs.

3.7 Annual check.

The annual check is to be carried out by the NMCS maintenance contractor or an
approved specialist. The following is a summary of the work:

1. Functional test of the full detection and release sequence using the test mode on
   the control panel. The discharge solenoid is not to be operated; the test is
   carried out by simulating the discharge signal.
2. Weigh each agent cylinder and record the weight on the cylinder test record sheet
   (Appendix C). Reject any cylinder that is more than 5% below the nominal fill
   weight.
3. Check the date of the last hydrostatic test on the cylinder neck. If the test is
   out of date, arrange for the cylinder to be replaced.
4. Visually inspect the discharge nozzles for damage or corrosion.
5. Check the condition of the flexible hoses and replace if the outer braid is
   damaged.
6. Check the control panel battery voltage and replace the batteries if below the
   manufacturer’s recommendation.

The agent used in Fire Suppression System DC-1 is argonite (IG-55). This is a blend of
50% argon and 50% nitrogen by volume, stored in the cylinder bank as a compressed gas
mixture. Argonite is electrically non-conductive and leaves no residue after discharge,
making it suitable for areas containing live electrical equipment and sensitive
electronics.

The Fire Suppression System DC-1 suppression_agent is listed as argonite (IG-55) in the
code. This remains the current approved agent for this system. No change to the agent
type is permitted without a full re-engineering review and approval from the Fire Safety
Manager.

When replenishing agent cylinders, use only supplier-certified argonite (IG-55) meeting
BS EN 15004-1. Do not top up cylinders with argon or nitrogen separately. The cylinder
bank for DC-1 comprises twelve 80-litre cylinders at a nominal fill pressure of 200 bar
at 15°C. The calculated design concentration for the protected volume is 38.2% by
volume. This concentration is maintained within the room for a minimum of 10 minutes
after discharge.

Cylinder pressure must be checked monthly. The acceptable pressure range is 190 bar to
210 bar at 15°C. If the pressure is outside this range, refer to Section 3.8 fault
finding. A pressure drop of more than 5% over a single month should be investigated
immediately for a possible leak.

| Cylinder bank | Agent | Fill pressure (bar) | Design concentration (%) | Protected area |
|---------------|-------|----------------------|---------------------------|----------------|
| DC-1 | Argonite (IG-55) | 200 | 38.2 | Electrical switchroom, level 2 |
| B7-2 (historical) | Inergen (IG-541) | 200 | 37.5 | Comms room, level 1 |

The B7-2 system was decommissioned in 2020. Its agent specification is retained above
for reference only. Do not use the B7-2 figures for any current design calculation.

The Fire Suppression System DC-1 suppression_agent is listed as argonite (IG-55) in the code. Record status: current.

**3.11 Discharge testing procedure**

Discharge testing is carried out to verify that the agent reaches the required
concentration and that the distribution is even throughout the protected volume. This
test is not the same as the annual functional test described in Section 3.7; a discharge
test actually releases agent from the cylinders.

Discharge testing is only permitted under the following conditions:

1. The area is evacuated and secured.
2. The Fire Safety Manager has issued a permit to work.
3. The ventilation dampers are closed and confirmed sealed.
4. The discharge is monitored using the pressure transducers at the test points shown
   in Appendix D.
5. The building management system is set to alarm mode so that a discharge signal is
   not misinterpreted as a real event.

The test procedure is as follows:

1. Isolate the system from the detection circuit using the key switch on the control
   panel.
2. Connect the test pressure transducers to the sample points. The sample points are
   located at ceiling level, at 1.0 m above floor level, and at the return air grille.
3. Record the ambient temperature and the room pressure before the test.
4. Operate the manual discharge control. The discharge solenoids will open and the
   agent will flow into the protected volume.
5. Record the pressure readings every 2 seconds for the first minute, then every
   10 seconds for the next 9 minutes.
6. After 10 minutes, record the final pressure readings and compare them with the
   predicted profile from the hydraulic calculation. The predicted profile is held in
   the system file, reference HYD-2016-044.
7. Ventilate the room thoroughly before allowing personnel to re-enter. The room must
   be ventilated for at least 30 minutes, or until the oxygen level is above 19.5% by
   volume.

**4.1 General**

All equipment rooms housing central plant assets shall be maintained within the environmental limits given in this Section. These limits are based on the manufacturer specifications for the installed equipment as well as on the requirements of the Building Management System (BMS) and the ventilation design. Where a more restrictive limit is given in a specific equipment manual, the more restrictive limit applies.

It is the responsibility of the Shift Supervisor to ensure that the environmental conditions in each equipment room are checked at the start of each shift and that any deviation from the limits in this Section is recorded in the Shift Log and reported to the Facilities Engineer on duty. The BMS provides continuous monitoring of temperature and humidity in the main plant rooms, but this does not replace the manual checks.

**4.2 Fire Suppression System DC-1 – Equipment Room Conditions**

The equipment room housing the Fire Suppression System DC-1 (the DC-1 room) contains the agent storage cylinders, the control panel, and the associated detection and actuation equipment. The room is located on the lower ground floor, adjacent to the main switch room.

The environmental limits for the DC-1 room are as follows:

| Parameter | Limit | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Minimum room temperature | 5 °C | Manufacturer specification. Current. |
| Maximum room temperature | 49 °C | Manufacturer specification. Current. |
| Relative humidity | 5% to 95% non-condensing | Manufacturer specification. Current. |
| Ventilation | Positive pressure, min 6 air changes per hour | See Section 4.5 |

The manufacturer specification requires Fire Suppression System DC-1 system_room_minimum_temperature to be 5 Celsius. Record status: current. This is the minimum temperature that shall be maintained in the DC-1 room at all times, including during periods when the heating system is being serviced or when the room is otherwise unoccupied.

If the room temperature is predicted to fall below the minimum limit, the Shift Supervisor shall arrange for temporary heating to be provided. Under no circumstances shall the system be taken out of service because of low temperature unless the temperature has actually fallen below the limit and the manufacturer has been consulted.

**4.3 Temperature Monitoring Procedure – DC-1 Room**

The temperature in the DC-1 room is monitored continuously by the BMS using the sensor located on the wall adjacent to the control panel. The BMS alarm is set at 6 °C and 48 °C.

In addition to the BMS monitoring, a calibrated portable thermometer shall be used to verify the room temperature at the following times:

1. At the start of each day shift, before any work is carried out in the room.
2. After any maintenance work that involves opening the room door for more than 30 minutes.
3. After any event that may have affected the room heating or ventilation, such as a power cut or a fault on the heating system.
4. At the end of each week, the weekly temperature check shall be recorded in the Weekly Plant Room Checks log (Form WPR-07).

The portable thermometer is held in the plant room office, in the drawer marked "Calibrated Instruments". The thermometer is calibrated annually; the calibration sticker is on the back of the instrument. If the thermometer is not available, the Shift Supervisor shall use the BMS reading and note on the log that the reading was taken from the BMS.

**4.4 Cooling Tower 2 – General Description and Duty**

Cooling Tower 2 (CT2) is a forced-draught, counter-flow unit serving the main process cooling loop. It is located on the roof of the plant room block, adjacent to the chiller yard. CT2 is the primary tower for the summer duty period; Cooling Tower 1 is retained as standby and for winter trim loads.

The tower is constructed from galvanised steel sections with a GRP basin. The fill pack is PVC, installed in 2017. The fan is a six-blade axial unit, belt driven from a 15 kW motor. The motor is controlled by a variable speed drive (VSD) located in the MCC panel on the plant room wall.

The datasheet gives Cooling Tower 2 cooling_capacity_kw as 1200 kilowatt. Record status: current. This rating is current and is the design figure used for all load calculations in this manual. The rating was confirmed at the last performance test (see Section 4.7) and shall be used for planning any future modifications to the cooling loop. The tower is not to be operated above this duty without written approval from the manufacturer.

Table 4.4.1 – CT2 Design Data (Current)

| Parameter | Value | Notes |
|-----------|-------|-------|
| Cooling capacity | 1200 kW | Manufacturer datasheet. Current. |
| Water flow rate | 45 l/s | Design flow. |
| Entering water temp | 32 °C | Summer design. |
| Leaving water temp | 27 °C | Summer design. |
| Fan motor | 15 kW, 4-pole | Belt driven. |
| Fan speed (max) | 720 rpm | Via VSD. |
| Basin capacity | 1,200 l | Working volume. |
| Drift loss | 0.02% of flow | Manufacturer limit. |

**4.5 Cooling Tower 2 – Routine Maintenance Schedule**

Routine maintenance of CT2 is carried out by the NMCS mechanical team. The schedule below is based on the manufacturer's recommendations and on operating experience since commissioning. Any deviation from this schedule shall be recorded in the CT2 maintenance log (Form CTM-08) and reported to the Shift Supervisor.

Table 4.5.1 – CT2 Routine Maintenance Schedule

| Item | Frequency | Task | Reference |
|------|-----------|------|-----------|
| Fan drive belts | Monthly | Check tension and condition. Adjust as required. | Section 4.6 |
| Fan motor bearings | Monthly | Grease via nipples (2 shots). | Section 4.6 |
| VSD filters | Quarterly | Clean air filters on cabinet. | Section 4.6 |
| Fill pack | Quarterly | Inspect for fouling or damage. | Section 4.6 |
| Basin | Monthly | Check water level, clean strainer. | Section 4.6 |
| Drift eliminators | Annually | Inspect and replace if damaged. | Section 4.6 |
| Gearbox (if fitted) | n/a | Not fitted to this unit. | – |

The monthly checks are carried out on the first working day of each month. If the first working day falls on a bank holiday, the check shall be carried out on the next working day. The Shift Supervisor shall sign the CTM-08 log after each check.

**4.6 CT2 – Detailed Maintenance Procedures**

**4.6.1 Fan Drive Belts**

Isolate the fan motor at the MCC panel before carrying out any work on the belts. Lock off the isolator and attach a warning notice. The belt tension is correct when the deflection at the centre of the top run is approximately 12 mm under moderate thumb pressure. Do not over-tension the belts, as this will shorten bearing life.

Inspect the belts for cracking, glazing, or fraying. Replace the belts as a matched set. When fitting new belts, do not use a lever to force them over the pulleys. The motor mounting bolts shall be loosened and the motor moved on its slide rails.

documents.content:
If fouling is light, the fill may be cleaned in place using a low-pressure water hose. Do not use high pressure, as this will damage the fill. If fouling is heavy, the fill pack shall be removed for cleaning or replacement. Refer to Section 4.8 for the fill pack replacement procedure.

**4.6.5 Basin Water Level and Strainer**

The basin water level is controlled by a float-operated make-up valve. The normal operating level is marked on the side of the basin with a painted line. Check the water level during the monthly inspection; it should be approximately 25 mm below the overflow weir.

The strainer is fitted at the suction side of the circulating pump. Clean the strainer by removing the lid and lifting out the basket. Rinse the basket and check for damage. Refit and ensure the lid seal is in good condition.

**4.6.6 Drift Eliminators**

The drift eliminators are located above the fill pack, below the fan deck. Annual inspection requires the fan to be isolated and the access hatch on the fan deck to be opened. Check the eliminator blades for cracking, warping, or displacement. Replace any damaged sections. Drift eliminator sections are Part No. DE-CT2-01.

**4.7 CT2 – Refrigerant System**

CT2 is fitted with a packaged air-cooled chiller for the closed-circuit cooling duty. The chiller is located on the plant deck, adjacent to the cooling tower basin. This section covers the refrigerant circuit, the refrigerant type, and the handling procedures.

**4.7.1 Refrigerant Type and Charge**

The chiller is charged with R-1234ze refrigerant. Cooling Tower 2 refrigerant_type is R-1234ze per the datasheet. Record status: current. This is the current and only approved refrigerant for this unit. Do not add or substitute any other refrigerant type without written authorisation from the NMCS Engineering Manager.

The refrigerant charge is 42 kg. The charge is recorded on the unit nameplate and in the chiller log book (Form CHL-02). A full charge record is kept in the plant office.

**Table 4.7.1 – CT2 Refrigerant Data**

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| Refrigerant type | R-1234ze |
| Charge weight | 42 kg |
| Design pressure (high side) | 15.5 bar g |
| Design pressure (low side) | 8.0 bar g |
| Safety valve set pressure | 17.0 bar g |
| Oil type | POE (as specified by compressor manufacturer) |
| Oil charge | 9.5 litres |

**4.7.2 Refrigerant Handling – General Precautions**

R-1234ze is a low-GWP (global warming potential) HFO refrigerant. It is classified as mildly flammable (A2L). The following precautions apply when handling this refrigerant:

- No smoking or naked flames in the vicinity of the chiller or any open refrigerant circuit.
- Work on the refrigerant circuit shall only be carried out by persons holding a valid F-Gas Handling Certificate (Category I or II as appropriate).
- The area around the chiller shall be well ventilated. If working indoors, ensure the area is mechanically ventilated.
- Use only refrigerant recovery equipment that is rated for HFO refrigerants. Do not mix recovery hoses or cylinders between different refrigerant types.
- Refrigerant cylinders shall be stored upright, secured, and in a cool, dry place. Do not store cylinders in direct sunlight.
- Spillages of liquid refrigerant can cause frostbite. Wear appropriate PPE, including insulated gloves and safety goggles.

**4.7.3 Leak Detection**

Leak testing of the refrigerant circuit shall be carried out in accordance with the F-Gas Regulation requirements. The chiller is fitted with a refrigerant leak detection system which alarms at a concentration of 10 ppm. The alarm is connected to the BMS.

This section covers the operation and maintenance of the main electrical distribution equipment in the central plant. It is intended for use by NMCS technicians and authorised contractors only. All work shall be carried out in accordance with the latest edition of BS 7671 (IET Wiring Regulations) and the Electricity at Work Regulations 1989.

- Obtain a Permit to Work (Form EL-01) for any work on live conductors or where there is a risk of inadvertent contact with live parts.

**6 PUMPS, VALVES AND PIPING SYSTEMS**

**6.1 General**

This section covers the routine operation and maintenance of the pumps, valves and piping systems installed within the Central Plant. It is to be read in conjunction with the relevant manufacturer's literature held in the plant office (drawing room, shelf B, binders P-01 to P-09). Where a conflict exists between this manual and the manufacturer's instructions, the manufacturer's instructions shall take precedence for equipment-specific details, but any deviation from the procedures herein shall be recorded on Form MP-04 and notified to the duty shift manager.

All work on plant items shall be carried out by competent persons. Isolation of any item for maintenance shall be in accordance with the Permit to Work system (Form PTW-01) and the site isolation procedure (Section 2 of this manual). Refer to the electrical isolation schedule for the relevant pump motor or valve actuator before commencing work.

**6.2 Pump Maintenance – General**

The following general procedures apply to all centrifugal pumps covered by this manual unless a specific exception is noted in the individual pump data sheets (Section 6.4).

**6.2.1 Routine Checks (Weekly)**

- Check pump for unusual noise, vibration or leakage from mechanical seal or gland.
- Check bearing housing temperature by hand. If too hot to hold (approx. 60°C or above), report and investigate.
- Check that the pressure gauge readings at suction and discharge are within the normal operating range noted on the pump data sheet.
- Check that the pump is not running dry. Confirm flow via the local flow indicator or duty point on the system.
- Visually check coupling alignment and condition of coupling guard.

**6.2.2 Lubrication**

Bearings are grease-packed and require no routine addition under normal service. The grease nipples shall be given one or two shots of grease (grade: Shell Alvania RL3 or equivalent) every 3 months for motors up to 30 kW, and every 6 months for larger machines. Do not over-grease; this can cause overheating and premature bearing failure.

The oil bath on the larger pumps (P-301, P-302, P-401, P-402) shall be checked weekly and topped up with the specified oil (see Table 6.4.1). A full oil change shall be carried out annually, or when oil analysis indicates contamination.

| **Oil Grade** | **Application** |
|---|---|
| Shell Tellus S2 V 32 | Bearing oil baths, all pumps |
| Shell Omala S2 G 220 | Gearboxes, if fitted |

**6.2.3 Mechanical Seals**

A small amount of seepage (a few drops per hour) from a mechanical seal is normal and indicates that the seal is being lubricated and cooled. A steady drip or spray indicates seal failure and the pump shall be taken out of service at the next available opportunity. Seal replacement shall be carried out only by a competent fitter familiar with the seal type fitted. Record the seal type and replacement date on the pump history sheet (Form MP-02).

**6.2.4 Pump Alignment**

Flexible coupling alignment shall be checked at the following intervals:

- After any major overhaul or disturbance of the pump or motor.
- When excessive vibration is reported.
- As part of the annual maintenance shutdown.

Use a dial gauge or laser alignment tool. The allowable misalignment is 0.1 mm total indicated reading (TIR) at the coupling periphery for speeds up to 1500 rpm, and 0.05 mm TIR for speeds above 1500 rpm. Shims shall be used under the motor feet to correct alignment; do not use more than 3 shims under any one foot. Record final alignment readings on Form MP-03.

documents.title: Central Plant Operations Manual
documents.content:
**6.2.5 Vibration Monitoring**

Vibration readings shall be taken on all pumps and their drive motors using the handheld vibration meter (Brüel & Kjær 2239, located in the workshop cabinet, key held by the shift supervisor). Readings shall be taken at the bearing housings in the vertical, horizontal and axial planes. Record readings on Form MP-04.

| **Machine** | **Point** | **Alarm (mm/s RMS)** | **Trip (mm/s RMS)** |
|---|---|---|---|
| All pumps, 0–75 kW | Bearing housing, DE | 4.5 | 7.1 |
| All pumps, 0–75 kW | Bearing housing, NDE | 4.5 | 7.1 |
| All pumps >75 kW | Bearing housing, DE | 3.5 | 5.6 |
| All pumps >75 kW | Bearing housing, NDE | 3.5 | 5.6 |
| Drive motors, all sizes | Bearing housing | 4.5 | 7.1 |

If a reading exceeds the alarm level, repeat the measurement to confirm. If the reading is confirmed, increase the frequency of readings to weekly and inform the maintenance supervisor. If a reading exceeds the trip level, the pump shall be taken out of service and the cause investigated before further operation.

**6.2.6 Coupling Lubrication**

Flexible couplings (spider type, where fitted) require no lubrication. Gear-type couplings, where fitted (see individual pump data sheets), shall be lubricated with Shell Omala S2 G 220 grease every 6 months. Apply a sufficient quantity to fill the coupling cavity; do not overfill, as this can cause the coupling to overheat and throw grease.

**6.2.7 Safety Precautions – Rotating Equipment**

The following safety precautions apply to all work on pumps and associated rotating equipment:

- Isolate the pump electrically and mechanically (close and lock the suction and discharge valves) before commencing any work.
- Tag out the isolator with a personal danger tag and the pump control switch with a caution tag.
- Do not work on a pump while it is running. If work must be carried out on a running pump (e.g., taking vibration readings), ensure all guards are in place and do not wear loose clothing, ties, or jewellery that could become entangled.
- Ensure the coupling guard is in place before starting the pump. Do not operate the pump without the guard fitted.
- Use a suitable sling and lifting points when handling heavy components. Do not lift a pump by its coupling or piping.
- When draining oil, use a suitable container and dispose of the waste oil in the designated waste oil drum (located in the boiler house compound). Do not allow oil to enter the drains.
- When cleaning parts, use a degreasing agent suitable for the material. Do not use petrol or other flammable solvents.
- Be aware of hot surfaces. Pumps handling hot water (e.g., HWS circulating pumps) can have surface temperatures above 60°C. Use insulated gloves when working near these pumps.

**6.3 Air Handling Units (AHU-01 to AHU-06)**

**6.3.1 General**

The air handling units serve the office, laboratory and workshop areas. Each unit comprises a supply fan, a return air fan, a heating coil, a cooling coil (AHU-01, 02, 03, 05, 06 only), a filter section, and a fresh air intake. The units are located in the plant room on the roof of the main building, with the exception of AHU-04 which serves the workshop and is located at high level in the workshop itself.

**6.3.2 Routine Inspection**

The following inspections shall be carried out weekly:

- Check fan belts for condition and tension. A belt should deflect approximately 10 mm when pressed at the mid-point between pulleys. Replace worn or damaged belts.
- Check the drain pans for blockage. Clear any debris and ensure the drain traps are primed with water.
- Check the fresh air intake grilles for blockage by leaves or other debris.
- Check the condition of the flexible connections at the fan inlet and outlet for tears or leaks.
- Check the damper actuators for correct operation. The fresh air damper should open when the supply fan is running and close when it is not.

**CENTRAL PLANT OPERATIONS MANUAL**

**NMCS – Estates & Facilities Directorate**

**Issue 4 – February 2020** (partial re-issue, sections 6 and 7 only)

**Supersedes:** Issue 3 (June 2018) – Sections 6.4, 6.5, 7.1 and 7.2 amended. All other sections remain current as per Issue 3.

**Revision history (extract)**

| Issue | Date | Sections affected | Reason |
|-------|------|-------------------|--------|
| 1 | 03/2017 | All | First issue |
| 2 | 11/2017 | 3, 6.1, 6.2 | Update to pump seals; revised HWS temp set points |
| 3 | 06/2018 | 6.4, 6.5, 7.1, 7.2 | Control panel firmware update; revised alarm test intervals |
| 4 | 02/2020 | 6, 7 (partial) | Calibration method change; sensor replacement parts list |

Note: Section 6.3 (AHU inspections) is unchanged from Issue 3 and remains current.

---

**6.4 Control System – General**

The central plant control system comprises the main control panel (MCP-01) located in the boiler house, two remote I/O panels (RIO-1 in the roof plant room, RIO-2 in the workshop), and the associated sensors and actuators. The system is a direct digital control (DDC) type, with a local operator display on the front of MCP-01. There is no remote access to the system; all adjustments are made locally.

Operators shall not make changes to control settings without authorisation from the Senior Technician. Any change shall be recorded in the Control Settings Log Book (kept on the shelf inside MCP-01).

**6.4.1 Operator Display**

The display shows the following values in sequence (or on demand via the navigation keys):

- Outside air temp
- Flow and return temps for each heating circuit (HWS1, HWS2, LTHW)
- Header pressure (HWS)
- Boiler status (on/off, fault)
- Pump status and running hours
- AHU supply and return air temps
- Filter differential pressure (AHU-01 to 06)

The display is a backlit LCD type. If the display is blank but the panel is powered, check the backlight fuse (F5, 500 mA) before calling for support.

**6.4.2 Time Clocks**

The control system has a 7-day time clock for each heating circuit. The clocks are set to give occupied and unoccupied periods. Check the clock setting each month against a reliable time source (e.g., the speaking clock or a GPS-synced watch). The clocks do not auto-adjust for BST/GMT – this is done manually by the technician during the spring and autumn changeover. If the clock is more than 5 minutes out, reset it and note the drift in the log book.

---

**6.5 Calibration of Sensors**

**6.5.1 General**

All temperature sensors and pressure transducers connected to the control system shall be checked for accuracy on a 12-monthly basis. The results shall be recorded on the Sensor Calibration Record sheet (Appendix C of this manual).

A sensor is considered acceptable if its reading is within the tolerances given in Table 6-1. If a sensor is outside tolerance, it shall be recalibrated (where possible) or replaced. Do not adjust a sensor without first checking the reading against a reference instrument.

**Table 6-1 – Sensor tolerances**

| Sensor type | Range | Tolerance | Reference instrument |
|-------------|-------|-----------|----------------------|
| Duct air temp (PT100) | 0–60 °C | ±0.5 °C | Calibrated digital thermometer |
| Pipe temp (PT100) | 0–120 °C | ±0.5 °C | Calibrated digital thermometer |
| Outside air temp (PT100) | −10 to +40 °C | ±0.5 °C | Calibrated digital thermometer |
| HWS header pressure (4–20 mA) | 0–10 bar | ±0.1 bar | Deadweight tester or calibrated gauge |
| Differential pressure across filters (4–20 mA) | 0–500 Pa | ±10 Pa | Manometer |

documents.title: Central Plant Operations Manual
documents.content:
**6.5.2 Calibration Procedure**

Before starting any calibration work, isolate the sensor from the process where possible. For
duct and pipe sensors, remove the probe and allow it to stabilise at room temperature for at
least 10 minutes before comparing against the reference instrument. For pressure transducers,
close the isolating valve and vent the manifold to atmosphere to obtain a zero reading, then
apply a known pressure using the deadweight tester or a calibrated gauge.

Record the as-found reading on the Sensor Calibration Record sheet before making any
adjustment. If the sensor is within tolerance, record the reading and return the sensor to
service. If outside tolerance, attempt recalibration using the adjustment procedure in the
manufacturer's instruction leaflet (kept in the plant room filing cabinet, drawer 2). Where a
sensor cannot be recalibrated, order a replacement via the stores system and tag the faulty
unit with a red "OUT OF SERVICE" label. Do not leave a faulty sensor in service while waiting
for the replacement to arrive.

**6.5.3 Sensor Replacement**

When replacing a sensor, use only the type listed in the spares list (Appendix D). Check that
the replacement probe length matches the original before insertion. For duct sensors, ensure
the probe tip sits in the centre of the duct and is not touching the duct wall. For pipe
sensors, use the correct pocket and fill the pocket with heat-conducting compound before
inserting the probe.

After replacement, allow the sensor to stabilise for at least 15 minutes before checking the
reading against the reference instrument. Record the new sensor serial number and the date of
replacement on the Sensor Calibration Record sheet and in the log book.

---

**6.6 Control System Software and Firmware**

**6.6.1 General**

The control system runs on a proprietary platform supplied by the original control system
manufacturer. The software version currently installed is v4.2.1. This version has been in
service since March 2022 and has been stable. Do not upgrade or modify the software without
written authorisation from the Facilities Manager. Any proposed upgrade shall be reviewed
by the controls contractor and a risk assessment completed before work begins.

**6.6.2 Firmware Updates**

Firmware updates for the controllers (DDC panels) are issued occasionally by the manufacturer.
These updates are not automatically applied. The controls contractor shall assess each update
and advise whether it is applicable to this site. Updates that address a known fault or a
security vulnerability shall be prioritised. Other updates may be deferred until the next
planned shutdown.

Record all firmware updates in the log book, including the date, the version number before and
after the update, and the name of the engineer who carried out the work. A copy of the
manufacturer's release notes shall be filed with the log book entry.

**6.6.3 Backups**

A full backup of the control system configuration shall be taken every 6 months. The backup
shall be stored on a USB stick kept in the plant room safe and also uploaded to the shared
drive (folder: NMCS/Controls/Backups). The backup shall include the controller programs, the
graphics pages, and the trend logs.

After any significant change to the control system (e.g., a new time clock schedule, a change
to a set point, or a firmware update), a fresh backup shall be taken and the old backup
retained for at least 12 months. Do not overwrite the previous backup until the new one has
been verified as readable.
